title: Foreign Investors Pour a Record Rs 1.42 Lakh Crore Into Indian Stocks in November
excerpt: NSDL data show foreign buying through November 24 has passed every previous monthly record, reversing Rs 70,704 crore of selling in September and October.
body:
• Foreign investors bought Rs 1.42 lakh crore of Indian equities in November through November 24, according to NSDL data — after selling Rs 70,704 crore across September and October.
  • Buying of Rs 1.22 lakh crore between November 2 and 20 alone broke the previous monthly record of Rs 60,358 crore, set in November 2020.
  • The money went mainly into domestic-facing sectors: financial services drew Rs 43,102 crore in the first fortnight of November, followed by telecom (Rs 7,570 crore) and autos (Rs 7,551 crore).
  • For NRI investors: the buying is large-cap led, and analysts quoted below caution that near-term profit-booking is possible after the rally; foreign flows for 2026 as a whole remain negative despite November.

Foreign investors have returned to Indian stocks at a pace not seen before. Foreign institutional investors bought Rs 1.42 lakh crore of Indian equities in November through November 24, according to data from the National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL) reported by Outlook Money. Two months earlier, the same investors were heading the other way: they withdrew Rs 70,704 crore in September and October combined.

The scale of the reversal

By November 20, foreign portfolio investors had already put Rs 1.22 lakh crore into Indian equities for the month — the highest monthly total on record, surpassing the previous record of Rs 60,358 crore from November 2020, according to NSDL data reported by Upstox. The buying stepped up through the month: CNBC-TV18, citing NSE provisional data, reported net purchases of Rs 32,646.67 crore in the single week ending November 20, rising from Rs 4,864.68 crore on November 16 to Rs 10,308.42 crore on November 20. The same report put cumulative foreign buying at over $14 billion across 15 trading sessions, after more than $60 billion of selling during the market's earlier peak-to-trough decline, and said India had become the biggest recipient of foreign equity inflows among emerging markets in that period.

The rally that came with the money has been broad at the top of the market: the Sensex and the Nifty 50 gained 14.57 per cent and 13.72 per cent respectively over one month to the November 20 close, per Google Finance data cited by Upstox. Even so, November's buying has only narrowed the year's damage. Cumulative foreign outflows from Indian equities in 2026 stand at approximately Rs 1.73 lakh crore, down from nearly Rs 3 lakh crore a few weeks ago.

Why the money came back

Analysts point to several drivers rather than one trigger. A correction in AI-linked stocks in the US and Asia made India's comparatively AI-light market a diversifier; crude oil prices eased, with Brent trading around $90-95 a barrel in the November 20 period; and India's second-quarter earnings surprised positively — an Indian Express report citing Bank of Baroda's analysis of about 2,600 listed companies put their combined net profit up nearly 26 per cent year-on-year to a record Rs 4.5 lakh crore. Brokerages have turned constructive: Goldman Sachs upgraded Indian equities to Overweight with a December 2027 Nifty target of 28,500, Citi raised its end-2027 target to 28,000, and HSBC also moved to Overweight. Our earlier coverage tracked a similar call from JPMorgan, which set an end-2027 Nifty target of 29,000.

Where the money went

NSDL sector data for the first fortnight of November show the buying concentrated in domestic-demand sectors rather than technology: financial services Rs 43,102 crore, telecom Rs 7,570 crore, autos Rs 7,551 crore and consumer services Rs 6,519 crore. IT stocks drew Rs 5,080 crore and FMCG Rs 3,042 crore.

"Buying was focused on banks, telecom and consumer stocks, which means the money is shifting to domestic-specific growth areas instead of just being because of the need to exit AI stocks."

— Ravi Singh, Chief Research Officer, Master Capital Services

Will it last?

That is the open question. Ajit Mishra, senior vice-president of research at Religare Broking, told Outlook Money that record inflows could increase the possibility of near-term profit-booking after the rally, though he does not see a large-scale rotation to other Asian markets as an immediate threat, and expects selective profit-booking and sector rotation to be more likely than an outright exit. ArunaGiri N, founder and CEO of TrustLine Holdings, noted India's earnings growth of around 15-20 per cent compares with roughly 30 per cent in the US AI ecosystem and more than 50 per cent in South Korea and Taiwan — so if global AI spending keeps growing, India could again lose out on foreign allocations. What to watch next: December flow data, the rupee, crude prices, and whether third-quarter earnings hold up the case the November money was bought on.
